TechnicalOperational

How it started

January 2026. Bold.org already had structured backend events in ClickHouse. Engineers investigated them with SQL. I wanted to see if an agent could do the same — so I gave it read-only access. It worked. Then I kept connecting more systems.

Jan 2026
The experiment
Read-only on ClickHouse. Then Slack, Linear, PostHog, Grafana — small CLI wrappers while MCP was still emerging.
Weeks later
Company-wide
Engineering, product, support, ops, marketing and growth were all using it.
Today
~4B tokens / mo
Daily workhorse across Bold.org — not a side project.
Our internal agent at Bold.org

Bad · design safe local access earlier

3.5 entry points

Slack
@sherlog where people already talk
Linear
@sherlog on issues
Web
Authenticated app: sessions, search, chat
+0.5
sherlog CLI — BYOK agent interface + safe gateway to the same capabilities
One session, any surface. The CLI is powerful — I should have designed safe local access earlier so people's own harnesses could use company tools without seeing credentials.
Ugly · I chased architecture too long

Architecture: deliberately boring

Box 1
Server
Box 2
Worker
Box 3
API
Capabilities
One shared layer for hosted Sherlog and the CLI (BYOK). Permissions enforced here. Credentials never reach the model.
clickhouse grafana ga4 circuits gsc klaviyo ahrefs …
Inference
The company’s OpenAI subscription, plus OpenCode Go for open-source models and lighter tasks.

Ugly truth: I lost time chasing better boxes. “Adoption does not happen because the architecture is impressive. It happens when somebody sees the agent solve a problem they recognize.”

Good · read-only first

Started read-only.
Then we opened writes.

First
Strictly read-only
Every remote access was read. Don't trust the model to know when a write is safe — just don't give it write permission.
Then
Gradual writes
PRs. Dashboards. Ops tools. Still gated — not a free-for-all.
Now
Useful, not reckless
The agent can change things that matter — through the capabilities layer, with permissions.

Automations

CRON
“Every Monday, send me the weekly report on X.”
CIRCUITS
Durable multi-step flows
TRIGGERS
Slack message → start an agent
Real run
“How is the launch doing?” → 12-chart PostHog dashboard + weekly Slack report. ~21 min to full setup; first run ~5 min. Higher activation rate, lower volume.

A real bug

~6 min · diagnose
Support report→Stale cache, silent success→Fix + PR
Valid referral — neither student got their 500 Bold Points.
Worker read a stale, pre-verification profile from cache. Job returned success → no retry, no Sentry.
Sherlog implemented the fix: uncached primary DB read + regression test, and opened the PR.
~6 min diagnose
~25 min request → PR
merged next day
Bad · contribution paths weren't obvious
Good · close the feedback loop

It improves itself

01
Edits its own automations
02
Edits its own prompts & matchers
03
Opens PRs to its own repo
Own bug
Missed Grafana alert — matcher only read Slack top-level text; alert was in an attachment. Fixed Slack normalization, added tests, opened a PR. ~1 min diagnose · ~24 min to merged PR.

How to start yours

01
Go where people talkPut it in Slack, in shared channels. Make usage public: every answer is a demo someone recognizes.
02
Plug in real contextRead-only first. Connect the tools you already use with small, boring wrappers. Don't chase architecture.
03
Open writes carefullyOne capabilities layer for every surface. Permissions live there. Credentials never in the model.
